The comparison between `cis_lll->rx.payload_count / cis_lll->rx.bn` and `event_count` that happens multiple places, isn't something that I understand. Can you elaborate on how event count and `cis_lll->rx.payload_count / cis_lll->rx.bn` relate? 

Should/could the comparison (or at least the `cis_lll->rx.payload_count / cis_lll->rx.bn` calculation) be put in a named local variable or a function?

The comparison here relates to the text in the spec.:
```
The burst of payloads associated with the
CIS event where cisEventCounter has the value E shall consist of payloads
with cisPayloadCounter between E × BN and (E + 1) × BN - 1.
```

Regarding refactoring, it will be addressed in #63152.
What does these bitmasks represent?
The bitmasks are used to determine stall `pkt_seq_num` compared to last recorded/used `cis->pkt_seq_num` value. Added comment in code to explain the same.
Ditto with embedded test code

To test flush timeout, one side of the connnection needs to skip/drop ISO event transmissions/reception, otherwise the flush timeout implementation can not be validated to check for correct reception of ISO data sequence.
Surprisingly, here the `rx` and `tx` differ significantly. Is that intentional?

Yes, as peripheral first receive PDU and then transmit, the transmit flush is to be handle in next ISO event (interval). Hence, the function is named `payload_count_rx_flush_or_txrx_inc()`, only rx is flushed at the close of the radio event (or both tx and rx payload count are incremented on sucessful ack and reception, respectively).
When a calculation like this is modified several times like in this PR, that usually indicate that it's something that should be put into a function :)
Decided to refactor once interleaved packing implementation is in place, and take up the refactoring together: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/issues/63152
Why do we only include the PSN if we ignore it?

When PSN from HCI is ignored, ISOAL still needs to schedule it to successive ISO events, and this `pkt_seq_num` value is used to generate the PSN so that ISOAL implementation is not modified when ignoring PSN from HCI.

i.e. CONFIG_BT_CTLR_ISOAL_PSN_IGNORE implementation is ensuring no HCI ISO data is considered stale by ISOAL implementation.

So if the PSN from HCI is ignore, you are generating fake PSNs in the controller?

I see that the code seems to just be incrementing the PSN (e.g. `cis->pkt_seq_num++;`), but does that work properly if the host does not send an SDU per SDU interval? 

If ignoring PSN from HCI, shouldn't the packets just be put into some kind of FIFO and the ISOAL not care about the PSN at all? 

Finally, how does the timestamp come into picture here? If you ignore the PSN and the host sends an SDU with timestamp = 10000 and then afterwards an SDU with timestamp = 9000, then the latter SDU should be sent first, right?

> If ignoring PSN from HCI, shouldn't the packets just be put into some kind of FIFO and the ISOAL not care about the PSN at all?

ISOAL simply assigns a payload count that will be picked by the lower link layer, it does not maintain or check next sequence number. Lower link layer check the assigned payload count and decides to drop ISO PDU with stale payload count. Hence, to truely enqueue as a simple FIFO, fake sequence of sequence number that is not stale compared to current lower link layer event count has to be given to ISOAL.

> Finally, how does the timestamp come into picture here? If you ignore the PSN and the host sends an SDU with timestamp = 10000 and then afterwards an SDU with timestamp = 9000, then the latter SDU should be sent first, right?

PSN_IGNORE should not be enabled if host intended to use timestamp, and its clock is in sync with the controller clock. ISOAL will give a correct payload count for timestamp = 10000 and will give the same last payload count for SDU with timestamp = 9000. Later SDU will be dropped by the lower link layer as stale.

Alright, so PSN_IGNORE effectively also disables the use of timestamps from the host? 

When the PSN_IGNORE feature is disable, is the controller able to handle the case where the host sends the following at t=0 
SDU 1 with PSN 5 and timestamp 5000
SDU 2 with PSN 10 and timestamp 10000
SDU 3 with PSN 9 and timestamp 9000

Or will it drop SDU 3?

The implementation states this:

https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/1dc6a8aa13fa73f9276e411d46d72d983ede0487/subsys/bluetooth/controller/ll_sw/isoal.c#L1837-L1842

Hence in the case of your example, 5, 10 and 9, are handled such that they are enqueued towards LLL in same order with payload counts 5, 10 and 10, where SDU 3 will be dropped in the LLL.
I see, so packets are dropped on PSN based on the order they come in, rather than the actual value of it? So the host sending PSN 9 after PSN 10 will always get dropped?

@niag-Oticon could you confirm my understanding that `isoal.c` enqueues ISO SDU with same payload number/count when the out-of-order PSN is provided by Host?

@Thalley LLL discards/drops ISO PDU enqueued by ISOAL if they do not have correct order payload_count/number assigned to them (by ISOAL) corresponding to ISO SDU PSN value.

I don't fully understand the implementation of the fake packet sequence number. However to address the out of order SDUs focusing only on the ISO-AL implementation:
SDU 1 with PSN 5 and timestamp 5000
SDU 2 with PSN 10 and timestamp 10000
SDU 3 with PSN 9 and timestamp 9000

The ISO-AL was not designed for this. Underlying assumption is that this is not a realistic case according to specifications.

But if it was to happen with CONFIG_BT_CTLR_ISOAL_SN_STRICT enabled, given the present logic (Unframed):

SDU 1 at PSN 5 TS 5000      -----> PDU 5 Event 5 (Assuming that target event is 5 on input to ISO-AL)
SDU 2 at PSN 10 TS 10000  ------> PDU 10 Event 10
SDU 3 at PSN 9 TS 9000      ------> PDU 11 Event 11

If it was to happen with CONFIG_BT_CTLR_ISOAL_SN_STRICT enabled, given the present logic (Framed):

SDU 1 at PSN 5 TS 5000      -----> PDU 5 Offset 0 Event 5 (Assuming that target event is 5 on input to ISO-AL)
SDU 2 at PSN 10 TS 10000  ------> PDU 10 Offset 0 Event 10
SDU 3 at PSN 9 TS 9000      ------> PDU 11 Offset 2000 Event 11

Don't we have `#define`s for the pb_flags?
there are defines but bit mask is used to check for combination of BT_ISO_START and BT_ISO_SINGLE values here. Added comments in code to explain the same.

It doesn't really make sense to use `BT_ISO_START` in the comments and then a literal value in the code. The reader will not know the relevance between the comment and the code. 

I strongly suggest to either use literal values in both comment and code (e.g. 0x01) or defined values in both (e.g. BT_ISO_START).
This applies to all similar places
It is either `!(pb_flag & 0x01)`  or `((pb_flag == BT_ISO_START) || (pb_flag == BT_ISO_SINGLE))`, former being less compare and branch instructions, and constant execution time.

`!(pb_flag & 0x01)` is indeed a minor optimization, and I'm not opposed to using that, but the comment you've supplied does not really tell the story that `!(pb_flag & 0x01)` and `((pb_flag == BT_ISO_START) || (pb_flag == BT_ISO_SINGLE))` is the same. 

Perhaps something like 
```
If pb_flag is BT_ISO_START (0x00) or BT_ISO_SINGLE (0x02) then we can simply check if the pb_flag is an even value, and then check that...
``` 

Since you are referring to the BI_ISO_START etc. values, then `pb_flag & 0x01` reads as `pb_flag & BT_ISO_CONT` (as BT_ISO_CONT == 0x01).
